content: The principles of human rights are reinforced by international standards for tuberculosis care, guidelines on HIV/AIDS and human rights, and the Patients’ Charter for Tuberculosis Care. These frameworks emphasize the right to receive treatment without stigma, prejudice, or discrimination from healthcare providers and authorities. Protecting the human rights of people who inject drugs (PWID) is essential to ensuring equitable access to healthcare. Programs should collaborate with other sectors and promote enabling factors to create a supportive environment for delivering comprehensive care to PWID. This includes ensuring access to justice for PWID and reducing their vulnerability to tuberculosis (TB), HIV, viral hepatitis, and other infections. In some settings, individuals who use or inject drugs are detained in compulsory drug detention or rehabilitation centers, where they are often supervised by custodial staff and have limited access to healthcare services. These detainees may face physical punishment and treatments that are neither evidence-based nor aligned with human rights principles. Relapse rates after release from such centers are typically high. United Nations entities do not support these forms of detention and urge member states to close compulsory drug detention and rehabilitation centers. Instead, they advocate for voluntary, evidence-informed, and rights-based health and social services for PWID within the community. Access to quality healthcare is a universal and fundamental human right, which includes the right of individuals who use drugs to receive appropriate, high-quality healthcare without discrimination. Healthcare providers and institutions must adhere to medical ethics and the right to health when serving PWID. PWID should not be denied treatment for TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, or drug dependence, nor should they be excluded from accessing needle and syringe programs (NSPs). Additionally, PWID must be able to access healthcare services without fear of police harassment, arbitrary arrest, stigma, discrimination, or other exclusionary practices. The effectiveness of the recommendations in this guidance depends on the design of services that maximize access for PWID, ensuring they are acceptable, high-quality, and widely implemented. Poor-quality or restricted services will significantly limit the individual and public health benefits of these recommendations. Access to justice is a critical priority for PWID, given their frequent interactions with law enforcement due to the criminalization of drug use in many countries. Justice includes protection from arbitrary police harassment, arrest, and detention; the right to a fair trial; freedom from torture and inhumane treatment; police protection when PWID are victims of crime; and the right to the highest attainable standard of health, even in prisons or other closed settings. High incarceration rates among PWID are common in many countries, and those not incarcerated often face regular contact with law enforcement. Protecting the human rights of PWID, including their rights to self-organize, employment, housing, and healthcare, requires collaboration between healthcare, social welfare, and criminal justice agencies, including those managing prisons. Detention in closed settings must not impede the right to dignity and health. The acceptability of services for PWID is a key determinant of their effectiveness. Interventions to reduce the burden of TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis among PWID must be respectful, acceptable, appropriate, and affordable to recipients. Some services for PWID may lack expertise in TB, HIV, or viral hepatitis, while specialized services for these conditions may not be acceptable or appropriate for PWID. Therefore, building service capacity across all fronts is necessary to adopt a people-centered approach. Collaboration between health services, PWID networks, and peer workers in service design, delivery, and evaluation is an effective strategy. Mechanisms for regular feedback from service users to providers can improve the acceptability of services. It is crucial that data and medical records identifying individuals as drug users are used solely to monitor disease burden and improve service quality, and not shared with law enforcement agencies. Health literacy among PWID may be inadequate, and concerns about treatment side effects may hinder their decision-making regarding disease prevention, healthcare-seeking, and treatment initiation. To address this, health services should routinely provide accurate, evidence-based, and non-judgmental information to PWID about the prevention, care, and treatment of TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis. This information can also be disseminated through community networks and peer workers, addressing concerns about comorbidities, treatment side effects, and social barriers such as stigma, discrimination, and criminalization. Similarly, healthcare providers and prison staff may lack knowledge of PWID’s health and social care needs. Training for staff in community and prison health services is essential to improve understanding and capacity to prevent and treat HIV, TB, and viral hepatitis among PWID. PWID often experience multiple comorbidities, including high rates of TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and mental health conditions, often in the context of marginalization and deprivation. Integrating services significantly improves access to collaborative TB/HIV activities for the general population and provides people-centered prevention, care, and treatment for PWID with complex health and social care needs. Integrated services enhance communication, multidisciplinary care, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. Programs should aim to deliver integrated services for PWID in ways that foster trust and are informed by PWID themselves. When full integration is not feasible, strong links between health and social services working with PWID should be established and maintained. The process of updating the WHO 2008 policy guidelines followed the recommendations of the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. A Joint Steering Group, comprising representatives from WHO, UNAIDS, and UNODC, oversaw the process, along with an External Guideline Group that included policymakers, experts in TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and drug-use services, donor agencies, and representatives from PWID networks. Feedback was solicited and incorporated into the final document, ensuring that the recommendations were evidence-based and aligned with human rights principles.
